title: Nanda's vanity
hookLine: the half-brother confesses he was vain and restless until he learned (Theragatha, Nanda)

cards: In one sutta, Nanda comes to the Buddha in pressed robes, with ointment around his eyes and a glazed, shining bowl in his hands. He's the Buddha's half-brother, son of the aunt who raised them both.

The Buddha looks at him and says, in effect: this isn't fitting for someone who left home out of faith. Go live in the forest, wear robes made of rags, and stop caring about the pleasures of the senses.
Later, Nanda made his own song about who he'd been.

teach.b: First, the confession. Nanda's verses in the Theragatha are short, and they open without a defense. Through careless attention, he says, I was given to adornment.
I was restless and fickle, burning with desire. No excuse about youth or family. Just: I was vain.

Through the skillful means of the Buddha, kinsman of the sun, he says, I practiced properly and pulled my mind out of the pull of becoming. Third, what skillful means meant in his case. The Udana tells the story.
Nanda wants to leave the order. He can't stop thinking of a young Sakyan woman who, as he left home, asked him to come back soon.
So the Buddha takes him, the story says, to a heaven, and shows him heavenly women more beautiful than anyone he's seen. Nanda admits the woman at home no longer compares.
The Buddha promises him such company if he practices, and Nanda practices, for a reward.

teach.h: A HIRED HAND, WORKING FOR WAGES.
teach.b: The other monks find out and call him a hired hand, working for wages. Ashamed, he goes off alone, practices in earnest, and is freed. Then he releases the Buddha from the promise.
He no longer wants the prize.

teach.h: THE SONG LEAVES THE PRIZE OUT.
teach.b: Fourth, what his song leaves out: no heaven, no prize, no teasing monks.
Only the plain admission and the plain gratitude. The story is strange and vivid. The song is spare.
A man who once dressed for an audience sings verses with nothing dressed up.

how: In Theravada teaching, Nanda's story is told as an example of the Buddha meeting a student where he is, and his verses sit among the Theragatha's songs of the early monks.

o: the pride in looks that Nanda's song confesses
Nanda's pride in his fine singing voice
Nanda's boast of being the Buddha's brother

games.q: Nanda's song and story: tap the pairs.
p: pressed robes and a shining bowl
opens: I was given to adornment

s: Nanda's own verses tell the story of the heavenly women
the Udana tells it. his song names only his vanity and the Buddha's skillful means.
Nanda first practiced for a reward
in the Udana he practices for the promised prize, until the other monks call him a hired hand.
Nanda held the Buddha to his promise in the end
once freed, he goes to the Buddha and releases him from it.

games.q: you're Nanda. the other monks are calling you a hired hand, practicing for a prize. what do you do?
o: leave the order and go home to the woman who's waiting.
go off alone and practice in earnest.
argue that a promise is a promise.
games.why: in the Udana, Nanda is ashamed, withdraws and practices in earnest, is freed, and then releases the Buddha from the promise.

practice: Ask quietly what you polish so people will see it, a look, a title, a way of seeming busy, a carefully chosen photo, and let one come, not to punish yourself. Name it simply, the way Nanda did: I was vain about this.
If something sits under it, a wish to be loved or to feel safe, breathe with it for a moment, without needing to fix it.

wordCard.voice: Nanda's vanity. The Buddha's half-brother, who once dressed for an audience, opens his song with a plain confession. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: I was vain. Nanda's song starts with the trouble and doesn't hide it. See you tomorrow.
